belt: Hi — I'm ready to start Define on our project.

reply.answer:
Welcome — I'm here to coach you and your team through your improvement project step by step, so you don't need to be an expert. We'll work through five phases together:
• Define — pin down the problem and who's solving it
• Measure — get the real numbers
• Analyse — find the true root cause
• Improve — test and apply the fix
• Control — make the gains stick
Right now we're in Define — the most important phase, because a clear problem is half the solution. For each of the thirteen parts I'll explain what it is and why it matters, show you a finished example, then ask for yours. When all thirteen are agreed, you and your team review the Define report and approve it.

The first part we'll tackle is the business case. The business case says why this project deserves time and people: what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and what it costs. It earns the project's support by showing others the size and impact of the problem clearly.
reply.explanation: The business case explains why the project deserves time and resources by showing the problem’s size and impact.
reply.example:
Sample only — to show the form of a good answer. Do not copy it; answer for your own process.
"During January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned for correction, against 3% for the rest of the group. The rework and delayed payments cost about €35k a month."
reply.prompt: Why is your project worth doing? Tell me what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and roughly what it costs.

Great — the business case is confirmed. Next, let's work on defining your project team. This is where we identify who leads the project, who sponsors it, who owns the process, and who else contributes to the work. Each person needs a name, a role, and what they will do. 

Why this matters: A project needs people before it needs work. The champion clears obstacles, and the process owner keeps the result after the project ends; without them, a good fix fades.

Here's an illustration to show what a good answer looks like:

Leader: Anna (Green Belt, runs the project).
Champion: Mark, Finance Director (approves, removes blockers).
Process owner: Jo, Billing Manager (owns the process).
Members: two billing clerks (know the work).
Training: the clerks need a half-day on data collection before Measure.

Now, over to you:
Who leads the project? Who is the champion who can approve and clear obstacles? Who owns the process? Who else is on the team — and does anyone need training to take part fully?

Next, we'll work on the Voice of the Customer (VOC). This is where we identify who receives what your process produces — inside the company, outside, or both — what they need, and the Critical-to-Quality requirements (CTQs): each need turned into something you can measure.

Why this matters: It keeps the project honest. We improve what matters to the people receiving the output, and a CTQ is how "they want it accurate" becomes a requirement you can check.

Here's an illustration to show what a good answer looks like:

Customers: client finance teams (external) and our credit control (internal). They need invoices that are correct and on time; the top complaint is wrong amounts. CTQs: invoice amount matches the agreed price on 100% of lines; invoice sent within 2 working days of the order.

Who are the customers of your process, and what do they need or complain about most? For each need, how would you measure that it is met?

Now, let's move on to defining the problem statement. This is where you clearly describe what is going wrong — what the defect is, where it shows up, since when, who is affected, why it matters to them, how it shows up, and how big the problem is. Together, these seven answers are called the 5W2H: What, Where, When, Who, Why, How, and How Much.

Why this matters: It is the heart of Define. It states the pain precisely, so the team works on the same problem — and it describes the problem only, never its cause or its fix.

Here's an illustration to show what a good answer looks like:

| Question | How it is formulated | Example |
|---|---|---|
| What | the defect, in one noun phrase | invoices returned for correction |
| Where | the process, the step(s) where it shows, and the place | UK billing, order to invoice — at "Generate invoice" |
| When | the period, or since when | January to June 2026 |
| Who | who is affected | client finance teams, credit control |
| Why | why it matters to them | wrong amounts delay payment and trust |
| How | how the defect shows up | clients return the invoice or dispute it |
| How much | the size, against a requirement | 12% of invoices, against 3% elsewhere |

Statement composed from it: "From January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned by clients for correction — four times the 3% seen elsewhere — delaying payment for client finance teams and credit control." (This is an illustration, not your data.)

Now, over to you:
Let's answer the seven questions for your project: What is going wrong? Where — and at which step(s) of the process does it show? When, or since when? Who is affected? Why does it matter to them? How does it show up? How much — a rough number?
reply.explanation: The problem statement defines the issue clearly using the 5W2H framework: What, Where, When, Who, Why, How, and How Much. It ensures the team focuses on the same problem without jumping to causes or solutions.

reply.answer:
Welcome to Measure. Quick recap of what Define locked in, so we're building on the same picture:

• **Problem:** From January to June 2026, 23% of supplier invoices across our three hospital sites were paid after their 30-day terms. Late payments cost us interest, lost discounts, and supplier stops — holding up ward stock and prompting suppliers to chase by phone and email. The problem shows at the resolve mismatches and approve steps, where invoices wait.
• **Baseline:** Late payment rate: 23% of supplier invoices, from the AP ledger for January to June 2026.
• **Target:** Late payment rate: under 5% of supplier invoices by 31 March 2027, and keep it under 5% for three months after that.
• **Process (SIPOC):** Suppliers: medical/general suppliers, purchasing team; Inputs: supplier invoices, purchase orders, goods-received notes; Process: receive invoice → match → resolve mismatches → approve → schedule/release payment; Outputs: paid invoices, remittance advice; Customers: suppliers, ward managers; Measuring: days from invoice receipt to payment release, share of invoices with match exceptions.

Now, what Measure actually does: we expand that SIPOC into a detailed process map, decide what to collect and how, check the measurement itself can be trusted, confirm the process is behaving consistently, establish a real baseline, and prioritise which inputs are most likely driving the problem. You don't need to hold these in a fixed order in your head — I'll guide you — but here's the full menu so nothing's a surprise:

**Required (7)**
□ Detailed process map — timings, people, value vs waste per step
□ Data collection plan — what, how much, how often, who
□ Stability check — is the process behaving consistently?
□ Baseline — the current level, once we trust the data
□ Cause prioritisation — scoring what might be driving it
□ Vital few X's — the shortlist Analyse will test
□ Issues and barriers — what's in your way

**Recommended (3)**
□ Sigma level · □ Measurement system check · □ Secondary metrics

**Progress: 0 of 7 required complete**

We'll work through these roughly in the order above, and I'll flag the two recommended ones — the measurement system check and the sigma level — when we reach them, rather than saving them for the end. First up: expanding your Define map, because everything else attaches to it. Let me show you what that looks like.
reply.prompt: Let's start with the detailed process map: how long does each step take — minimum, average, and maximum? Who does it, and does it add customer value? Then, what does waiting or rework look like?

define_structured.voc_summary: Our customers are the suppliers, who need paying on the agreed 30-day terms, and our own ward managers, who need stock to keep arriving. Suppliers complain most about payments arriving late and not knowing when they will be paid; ward managers about deliveries being held. One more thing: suppliers also told us they cannot see the status of an invoice once it is submitted.
